newsitem.title: USA: Dollar mostly lower after U.K. interest rate hike boosts pound.
newsitem.headline: Dollar mostly lower after U.K. interest rate hike boosts pound.

text.p: The dollar tumbled to a 19-month low against the pound Wednesday after Britain's finance minister unexpectedly raised British interest rates.

The pound also jumped to its highest level against the mark in almost two years after Kenneth Clarke, the chancellor of the exchequer, authorised a quarter-point increase in British rates to 6 percent, the first rise since February 1995.
Hurt by its slide against the pound, the dollar fell further from Tuesday's 42-month high of nearly 115 Japanese yen.
"Certainly dollar/sterling was a large part of it," said John McCarthy of ING Barings Capital Markets. He said profit-taking also drove the dollar lower against the yen.
The pound extended its recent rally and touched $1.6345, its highest level since March 1995. It closed at $1.6330 late in New York, up from $1.6104 late on Tuesday.
The dollar fell to 114.13 yen from 114.35 yen on Tuesday.
But the dollar managed to recoup early losses against the mark as the German currency fell against the buoyant pound and the yen. It edged up to 1.5114 marks from 1.5105 marks late on Tuesday.
After months of resisting requests from the Bank of England, Britain's central bank, Clarke surprised the markets by authorising the rate rise ahead of general elections due by next May.

Clarke's action, meant to ward off inflation while keeping Britain's economy growing, also lured investors seeking higher yields on their investments. Rates have been steady or moving lower in the United States, Japan and Germany.

"It was already up. Then of course the rate move was well accepted by the market and they pushed sterling even further, sterling/mark as well," said Stephen Flanagan, vice president at Credit Agricole in New York.

While higher rates could raise mortgage payments for millions of Britons and further erode confidence in the already embattled Conservative government, Clarke said he was determined to nip possible inflation in the bud.

"It's interesting because it sort of gives the impression they are content with the rise in sterling ... and perhaps we might even see higher levels from here," said Debra Doerr-Larsen, assistant vice president at Commerzbank in New York.

The mark got a short-lived boost against some European currencies amid ongoing questions about whether the European Union will block a French plan to transfer money from state-owned French Telecom to the national budget to meet fiscal conditions for entry to Europe's single currency.

A member Germany's central bank, Raimut Jochimsen, criticised the French plan in a BBC television interview Wedenesday, saying it sent the wrong signal to other countries ahead of the planned single European currency.
Dollar traders all but ignored a government report showing the U.S. economy slowed to a 2.2 percent rate of growth in the third quarter from 4.7 percent in the second quarter.
Elsewhere, the dollar fell to 1.2553 Swiss francs from 1.2560 late on Tuesday. It fell to Canadian $1.3413 from C$1.3443.
